title: Tense and Aspect
full_title: Tense and Aspect: Time in English
tagline: Time, tense and aspect, simple and progressive, the present perfect, the present perfect progressive, narrative tenses, the future, past habits, English tenses and Chinese 了, 过 and 着, and choosing tenses in real texts
summary: English verbs carry two kinds of information about time: tense, which places a situation in the present or the past, and aspect, which shows whether it is seen as complete, in progress or connected to a later point. Chinese expresses these ideas with particles such as 了, 过 and 着 and with time words, so English tenses are among the hardest parts of the language for Chinese learners. This course builds the whole system, from the meaning of the simple and progressive forms to the present perfect, the narrative tenses, the many ways of talking about the future, and how writers choose tenses in real texts.
overview: This course is about how English verbs talk about time. It starts with a simple model: a line with the moment of speaking on it, the time of the event, and sometimes a third point that the speaker looks from. With this model it builds the whole system step by step — the simple and progressive forms, the present perfect and the present perfect progressive, the past progressive and past perfect of stories, the many ways of talking about the future, and *used to* and *would* for past habits. It ends with two chapters that look at the system from outside: how it compares with Chinese 了, 过, 着 and 在, and how writers choose and keep tenses in real texts.

Tense and aspect are in almost every English sentence, so mistakes here are frequent and easy to notice. *I have seen him yesterday*, *I am living here since 2020* and *When I will arrive, I call you* are all understandable, but each one tells a listener that the speaker has not yet mastered the system. More importantly, the forms carry meaning: *She lived in Paris* and *She has lived in Paris* say different things about now, and *I'll see him* and *I'm seeing him* say different things about the plan.

The course builds on the present simple, present continuous, past simple and first future forms of *Core Grammar*, and does not teach their forms again. Each chapter gives the forms in tables, states the rules of use with their limits, and compares each form with its neighbours. Every chapter has a note on English and Chinese, worked examples, quick checks and graded exercises with full answers. The chapters are best read in order up to the narrative tenses; after that, the future and past habits can be read in either order.

For Chinese speakers the main difficulty is not the forms but the idea that the verb must be marked every time. Chinese shows time with words such as 昨天 and 已经, and aspect with particles that are often optional; English requires a choice of tense and aspect in every finite verb. A second difficulty is that the Chinese particles look like English tenses but are not: 了 marks a completed or bounded event, not past time, and 过 is close to the experiential present perfect only part of the time. The best approach is to learn what each English form means, and then to check your own writing for one form at a time.
outcomes: Explain the difference between time, tense and aspect, and name the tense and aspect of any finite English verb phrase.
Choose between simple and progressive forms in the present, past and future, and recognise the state verbs that usually resist the progressive.
Choose between the present perfect and the past simple, including with *just*, *already*, *yet*, *ever*, *for* and *since*, and mark the British and American differences.
Choose between the present perfect simple and progressive, for example *I've read* and *I've been reading*.
Tell a story with the past simple, past progressive, past perfect and past perfect progressive, each in its usual role.
Choose between *will*, *be going to*, the present continuous and the present simple for the future, and form the future progressive and future perfect.
Use *used to* and *would* for past habits and states, and keep them apart from *be used to* and *get used to*.
Explain how Chinese 了, 过, 着 and 在 differ from English tenses, and correct the tense errors that come from translating them directly.
Keep tenses consistent in a paragraph, and choose the usual tenses for stories, news reports, emails and academic writing.

chapters.title: Time, tense and aspect
chapters.summary: The difference between time and tense, the two tenses and two aspects of English, and a timeline model with event time, reference time and speech time.

chapters.title: Simple and progressive
chapters.summary: What the progressive adds — an action in progress, temporary or unfinished — and why state verbs such as *know*, *own* and *belong* rarely take it.

chapters.title: The present perfect
chapters.summary: *Have* + past participle for experiences, recent events with present results and situations continuing up to now, and the contrast with the past simple.

chapters.title: The present perfect progressive
chapters.summary: *Have been* + *-ing* for activities up to now, *for* and *since*, and the choice between *I have read* and *I have been reading*.

chapters.title: Narrative tenses
chapters.summary: The past progressive for background, the past perfect for earlier events, and how the narrative tenses work together in a story.

chapters.title: The future
chapters.summary: *Will*, *be going to*, the present continuous and the present simple for the future, the future progressive and future perfect, and the differences in meaning between them.

chapters.title: Past habits: *used to* and *would*
chapters.summary: *Used to* and *would* for past habits and states, and the different meaning of *be used to* and *get used to*.

chapters.title: English tenses and Chinese 了, 过 and 着
chapters.summary: How Chinese marks time and aspect with particles and time words, where these match English tenses and where they do not, and the tense errors that follow.

chapters.title: Choosing tenses in real texts
chapters.summary: How tenses are used in stories, news reports, emails and academic writing, and how to keep tenses consistent across a paragraph.

history.title: Wallis and the rule for *shall* and *will*
history.detail: John Wallis's *Grammatica Linguae Anglicanae*, a grammar of English written in Latin, stated that *shall* with *I* and *we* and *will* with other subjects simply predict, while the opposite pairs express promise or determination. Later grammarians repeated the rule, although usage never followed it closely.

history.title: Jespersen on time and tense
history.detail: The fourth part of Otto Jespersen's *A Modern English Grammar on Historical Principles* dealt with time and tense. Jespersen kept the notion of time apart from the verb forms that express it, and called the progressive the "expanded tenses".

history.title: Reichenbach's three points in time
history.detail: In *Elements of Symbolic Logic* the philosopher Hans Reichenbach described the tenses with three points: the point of speech, the point of the event and a point of reference. His model, used in this course, explains the difference between the past simple and the present and past perfect.

history.title: Vendler's verb classes
history.detail: In the article "Verbs and Times" the philosopher Zeno Vendler divided verbs into states, activities, accomplishments and achievements. The classes explain why *know* rarely takes the progressive and why *The train is arriving* means that it has not yet arrived.

history.title: Chao's grammar of spoken Chinese
history.detail: Yuen Ren Chao's *A Grammar of Spoken Chinese* treated 了, 着 and 过 as aspect suffixes of the verb, an analysis that later grammars of Mandarin developed further.

history.title: Leech's Meaning and the English Verb
history.detail: Geoffrey Leech's short book explained the meanings of the English tenses, aspects and modal verbs for teachers and advanced learners. Its third edition appeared in 2004.

history.title: Comrie's Aspect
history.detail: Bernard Comrie's *Aspect* gave the standard definition of aspect as the different ways of viewing the internal temporal constituency of a situation, and compared aspect systems across many languages, Chinese among them. His *Tense* followed in 1985.

history.title: Li and Thompson on Mandarin aspect
history.detail: Charles Li and Sandra Thompson's *Mandarin Chinese: A Functional Reference Grammar* described perfective 了 as marking a bounded event, sentence-final 了 as marking a currently relevant state, 过 as experiential and 在 and 着 as durative. The next year 朱德熙's 《语法讲义》 gave a parallel account in Chinese.

history.title: Tense and aspect counted in a corpus
history.detail: The *Longman Grammar of Spoken and Written English* by Douglas Biber and colleagues showed how often each tense and aspect is used in conversation, fiction, news and academic prose, and that the present perfect is more common in British than in American English.

references.title: Practical English Usage
references.note: Fourth edition. Clear entries on every tense and future form, with British and American differences; the first book to check a doubtful rule.

references.title: English Grammar in Use
references.note: Fifth edition. Self-study grammar for intermediate learners; its first thirty units practise the tenses covered in this course.

references.title: Meaning and the English Verb
references.note: Third edition. A short, readable account of what each tense and aspect means, for teachers and learners who want to understand the choices.

references.title: Longman Grammar of Spoken and Written English
references.authors: Douglas Biber, Stig Johansson, Geoffrey Leech, Susan Conrad and Edward Finegan
references.note: A corpus grammar: how often each tense and aspect is used in conversation, fiction, news and academic writing, and in British and American English.

references.title: The Cambridge Grammar of the English Language
references.authors: Rodney Huddleston and Geoffrey K. Pullum
references.note: The most detailed modern reference grammar; its chapter on the verb treats tense, aspect and the perfect with great care, and treats the perfect as a kind of tense.

references.title: Aspect
references.note: The classic introduction to aspect across languages, for readers who want to see where English and Chinese stand among the world's systems.

references.title: Mandarin Chinese: A Functional Reference Grammar
references.authors: Charles N. Li and Sandra A. Thompson
references.note: The standard English-language account of 了, 过, 着 and 在, used to check every comparison with Chinese in this course.

references.title: 语法讲义
references.note: A classic grammar of Mandarin in Chinese; its treatment of the verb suffixes 了, 着 and 过 and of sentence-final 了 is the Chinese-language reference for the contrastive notes.
